ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory pre-incorporation client due diligence and ongoing screening against: FINTRAC guidance under PCMLTFA; United Nations Security Council Consolidated List; Special Economic Measures Act (SEMA) sanctions schedules (including Russia, Belarus, Iran, Syria, Venezuela, DPRK, Myanmar, and others); Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act (Canada's Magnitsky) list; Canadian Radiated/Listed persons; and OFAC SDN List where USD-clearing or US-correspondent Swift LC/TT wire rails will be used. PEP classification follows FINTRAC categories (domestic PEP, foreign PEP, head of international organization, and family/close associates) triggering enhanced due diligence, beneficial ownership re-verification, and transaction monitoring. Banking counterparties will apply independent KYC and may request UBO declarations exceeding the 25% statutory threshold.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: BC Corporate Online / OneStop Business Registry (BC Registries portal, operated by the Registrar of Companies, British Columbia; NUANS name search mandatory prior to reservation)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Corporate names must be in English or French (or both) using only letters of the English alphabet, Arabic numerals, or a combination; corporate designators limited to 'Limited', 'Ltd.', 'Corporation', 'Corp.', 'Incorporated', 'Inc.' or French equivalents 'Limitée', 'Ltée' etc.; names must be distinctive and not cause confusion with existing BC, Canadian federal, or extra-provincial registered names; foreign-language names must include a full transliteration; a NUANS report is required to determine distinguishability; names deemed contrary to public interest or misleading are rejected.
prohibited_and_sensitive_tokens: Medical (potential conflict with Health Professions Act)
Health (potential conflict with medical regulatory bodies)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: BC name reservations under s. 23 BCA are valid for 56 days and are not extendable; re-filing is required upon expiry. Upon rejection, the applicant resubmits through BC Registries with additional distinguishing elements, letter(s) of consent from the relevant regulator (e.g., College of Physicians and Surgeons for 'Medical'), and trademark registration evidence. The incorporator may file a formal reconsideration request with the Registrar of Companies; if refused, judicial review may be initiated by petition to the Supreme Court of British Columbia under the Judicial Review Procedure Act, RSBC 1996, c. 241, and s. 27 BCA. The Registrar may also require a company to change its name under s. 26 of the BCA where the name is confusing or misleading, with a compliance deadline in the registrar's order.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Partially permissible: A BC-incorporated company must maintain a registered office and a records office in British Columbia at a physical street address (no P.O. box). A registered-office service provider or corporate agent may serve as the registered office, but mail-forwarding-only virtual offices are insufficient. For the instant medical device scope (sterile examination nitrile gloves, Class II medical device), a Health Canada Medical Device Establishment Licence (MDEL) and, where manufacturing occurs, a Medical Device Licence (MDL) are mandatory; the importer/distributor must have an actual Canadian establishment premises registered with Health Canada and pursue ISO 13485 (CMDCAS) certification, requiring significant physical commercial substance beyond a virtual office.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: 55% within the first 24 months of operations: Health Canada inspectors conduct regulatory inspections under the Food and Drugs Act and Medical Devices Regulations, ISO 13485 CMDCAS certification audits are on-site and unannounced follow-ups are possible, and CBSA and FINTRAC may inspect records for imported PPE and reporting-entity compliance.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Business Corporations Act (SBC 2002, c. 57), ss. 2-5 (incorporation), s. 11 (authorized share structure), s. 42 (registered office), s. 128-131 (directors), s. 173-176 (records office and corporate records); administered with the BC Regulation 221/2002.
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: British Columbia Registry Services, Corporate and Personal Property Registry, Ministry of Finance (via the one-stop BC Corporate Online portal)
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Notice of Incorporation (Form 1) filed under s. 5 of the Business Corporations Act, resulting in a Certificate of Incorporation; accompanied by Form 2 (Articles), Form 3 (Notice of Registered Office and Records Office) and Form 4 (Notice of Directors).
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No statutory minimum paid-up capital and no escrow account requirement under the BCA; a BC business corporation may be incorporated with one or more shares without par value, fully paid upon subscription. The subscribers' consideration may be cash, property, or past services.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: RESOLVED: 1. That the Articles filed with the Notice of Incorporation be adopted as the constating instrument and the corporate seal be approved. 2. That Shares No. 1 to 100 be allotted and issued to the subscriber named in the Incorporation Agreement as fully paid and non-assessable, and that share certificate No. 1 be sealed and delivered. 3. That the registered and records office of the corporation be established at the address stated in Form 3, and that the Registrar be notified under s. 42 BCA. 4. That the following officers be appointed: President, Secretary-Treasurer. 5. That the officers be authorized to open bank accounts at the corporation's principal bank and to execute all banking documents.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Name Reservation and Corporate Name Request
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: BC Registry Services, Corporate Online (CORES) name-request module
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Submit a Name Reservation Request via the BC Corporate Online portal. For an eponymous or descriptive name, obtain a preliminary name search to verify no conflict with existing BCA or extraprovincial registrants. If a trade name containing 'Sterile' is desired for medical-device branding, ensure it does not imply government endorsement. Direct submission is accepted; notarization of the request is not required for electronic filing, but a certified copy may be requested for records.
required_dossiers: Completed Name Reservation Request
Name search report or NUANS-equivalent BC search output
First and second preferred corporate names
Incorporator's contact details and signature block
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the name is rejected by the registrar, file an amended Name Reservation Request with a new first and second preferred name, or proceed as a numbered company under s. 5(2)(b) BCA with an assigned registration number.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Incorporator(s) with drafting by corporate legal counsel; no statutory pre-clearance required
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Draft the Articles in the prescribed Form 2 format, incorporating the authorized share structure, director count, quorum, pre-emptive rights, and transfer restrictions. Prepare the Incorporation Agreement executed by each subscriber evidencing share subscription. Prepare Form 3 (Notice of Registered Office and Records Office) and Form 4 (Notice of Directors) including each director's consent to act. All signatures may be electronic or wet-ink; scanned copies are archived in the company's minute book. No notarization or apostille is required for domestic incorporators.
required_dossiers: Form 2 Articles of Incorporation
Incorporation Agreement signed by subscribers
Form 3 Notice of Registered Office and Records Office
Form 4 Notice of Directors with directors' consents
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: Clerical defects are cured by re-execution of the affected schedule before filing; material inconsistencies between Articles and Incorporation Agreement require an amending agreement or withdrawal and re-filing.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Electronic Filing of Notice of Incorporation with Registry
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: BC Registry Services via Corporate Online (one-stop business registration)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Login to BC Corporate Online, select 'Incorporation: Apply for a Business Corporation', upload the completed Form 1 together with Form 2, Form 3 and Form 4, and remit the CAD 350 filing fee. The Certificate of Incorporation is issued electronically in PDF upon approval; retain the certificate for CRA registration and banking. If filing by paper, the completed forms are submitted to the Victoria registry office and payment is made by cheque; no notarization is required.
required_dossiers: Form 1 Notice of Incorporation
Form 2 Articles
Form 3 Notice of Registered Office and Records Office
Form 4 Notice of Directors with director consents
Evidence of fee payment (payment transaction receipt)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the registry issues a Notice of Query, respond within the stated statutory period (typically 30 days) by submitting amended schedules; if the application is refused, re-file with corrected share structure or change the jurisdiction of the records office and resubmit.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Inaugural Board Meeting and Pro-Forma Resolutions
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Board of Directors of the corporation
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Convene the first organizational meeting of the incorporator(s) and then the first board meeting. Adopt the pro-forma resolutions approving the Articles, issuance of shares, appointment of officers, establishment of the registered and records office, and selection of the corporate bank and auditor. Record minutes in the corporate minute book; issue share certificate No. 1 and enter share allotments in the register of members.
required_dossiers: Waiver of notice of first board meeting
Minutes of first board meeting adopting resolutions
Share certificate No. 1 and share register entries
Officer appointment forms and director consent acknowledgments
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: Failure to hold a valid first board meeting is cured by a subsequent unanimous shareholder consent resolution ratifying all organizational actions nunc pro tunc.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Canada Revenue Agency and Provincial Tax Registrations
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Canada Revenue Agency, Business Registration Online (BRO), and BC Ministry of Finance
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Using the incorporated company's legal name and Certificate of Incorporation, submit the Business Number (BN) registration through CRA's BRO portal. Electronically register for GST/HST where taxable supplies exceed CAD 30,000; register for the British Columbia Provincial Sales Tax (PST) account and, once employees are hired, for payroll source deductions and WorkSafeBC coverage. Upload corporate information and the registered office address as provided in Form 3.
required_dossiers: Certificate of Incorporation
Form 3 registered office details
Corporate banking account confirmation
Shareholder and director information for beneficial ownership reporting
Application for GST/HST, PST, and payroll accounts (RC1A or BRO intake)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If CRA flags the BN application, use the CRA Business Number Liaison Officer service to reconcile identity mismatches; if tax account registration is rejected due to missing incorporation data, rectify the corporate registry record and re-submit the BRO application.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Corporate Record Formation and Annual Registry Maintenance Setup
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Corporate secretary and BC Registry Services
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Establish the statutory corporate records at the records office: minute book, register of directors, register of members, register of allotments, and copies of all constating documents as mandated by ss. 173-176 BCA. Register the annual report due date based on the anniversary of incorporation. Confirm the records office location in British Columbia is accessible during business hours and notify the registrar of any change using Form 3. Keep securities registers compliant with the Canada Business Corporations Act transparency reporting insofar as applicable to BC extraprovincial operations.
required_dossiers: Minute book and corporate seal
Register of directors and register of members
Register of allotments and transfers
Certificate of Incorporation and Articles
Annual report calendar confirmation
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the regulator identifies missing records, complete the records retroactively through director resolution; late annual report filings may be cured by paying the late-filing penalty and filing the current annual report before the registry strikes the company.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Municipal Zoning and Local Business License for Light-Industrial Sterile Manufacturing
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Local municipality (City of Vancouver/Surrey or applicable BC city) Development and Licensing Department
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Submit an application for a municipal business licence under the applicable municipal bylaw to authorise the operation of a light-industrial glove-dipping plant. Verify zoning compliance for the premises in an industrial zone (such as M-1 or I-1) and obtain a building occupancy permit for the planned production lines. Submit floor plans, hazardous materials storage documentation, and a fire safety plan; if the facility uses a wet process, verify sanitary sewer discharge approval from the local engineering department. Provide proof of WorkSafeBC registration and a copy of the Certificate of Incorporation.
required_dossiers: Municipal business licence application form
Certificate of Incorporation and proof of BC registered office
Lease or proof of ownership of the industrial premises
Zoning compliance letter and floor plan
Fire safety plan and hazardous materials declaration
WorkSafeBC registration and proof of insurance coverage
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the municipality queries the licence, submit an amended application addressing zoning discrepancies; if zoning does not permit dipping lines, the remedy is to file for a minor variance with the Board of Variance or relocate to an appropriately zoned industrial unit and re-submit.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: Health Canada, Medical Devices Directorate (MDD), in coordination with the British Columbia Ministry of Health and the local municipal Building and Fire Departments; for environmental matters, Environment and Climate Change Canada and BC Ministry of Environment and Climate Change Strategy
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: Medical Device Establishment Licence (MDEL) and Medical Device Licence for Class II Sterile Examination Gloves under the Food and Drugs Act, RSC 1985, c. F-27, and the Medical Devices Regulations, SOR/98-282; supplemented by ISO 13485:2016 quality management system certification and a Canadian Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) compliance dossier

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.agency_name: British Columbia Ministry of Environment and Climate Change Strategy, Environmental Protection Division, under the Environmental Management Act (SBC 2003, c. 53); federal oversight by Environment and Climate Change Canada under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, 1999
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Potentially a 'Registration' category under Part 2.1 of the Environmental Management Act for moderate-risk industrial operations; a full Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) report is not normally required for glove-dipping lines unless involving significant discharge to sensitive receiving waters or hazardous waste thresholds, in which case the project is escalated to a detailed EIA review
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: Wastewater discharge must meet the BC Municipal Wastewater Regulation and the Environmental Management Act Schedule 1 effluent criteria, typically biochemical oxygen demand (BOD5) ≤ 45 mg/L and total suspended solids (TSS) ≤ 60 mg/L, with pH within 6.0-9.0; volatile organic compound (VOC) emissions must comply with the VOC Concentration Limits in the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, 1999 and any approved BC air emissions permit; hazardous waste, including coagulant and leachate streams containing residual nitrile polymer and curing chemicals, must be characterized, manifested, and disposed under the BC Hazardous Waste Regulation (BC Reg. 63/88) and the federal hazardous waste import/export rules if applicable

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: Fire safety certification by the local fire authority under the BC Building Code (fire separation, suppression, and egress requirements, NFPA 13-compliant sprinkler system where mandated); structural load inspection of high-volume dipping lines and driers issued by a licensed professional engineer; and WorkSafeBC occupational health and safety clearance covering WHMIS training, chemical protective equipment, emergency evacuation plans, hazardous materials storage limits, and electrical safety permits before production start.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) / Agence du revenu du Canada (ARC), via the Business Registration Online (BRO) portal at canada.ca; provincial tax administration for British Columbia is the Ministry of Finance, Consumer Tax Branch, and BC Corporate Registry for extraprovincial registration
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: A foreign corporation must first obtain a federal Business Number (BN) from the CRA through the BRO portal, with the program account suffix RC for corporate income tax, followed by applicable program accounts (e.g., GST/HST account starting with the BN plus a two-letter program identifier). For British Columbia, the corporation must also file an extraprovincial registration with BC Corporate Registry under the Business Corporations Act and obtain a BC incorporation/extraprovincial number; if the entity carries on business in BC and has a permanent establishment, it may need BC Corporate Income Tax registration with the BC Ministry of Finance. Required documents include the certificate of incorporation or equivalent foreign charter, registered office address, directors' information, and a completed RC348 or online BRO application; a GST/HST registration can be obtained simultaneously if taxable supplies are anticipated to exceed the registration threshold or if the entity voluntarily elects to register. A TIN for federal purposes is the Business Number (BN), and the GST/HST account number is a derivative code; Canada does not issue a separate VAT ID distinct from the BN.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: Canada does not operate a check-the-box regime comparable to the US. A corporation or foreign corporation is statutorily classified as a taxpayer subject to entity-level Part I tax, unless it is a qualifying 'Canadian-controlled private corporation' (CCPC) using the small business deduction, or a non-resident corporation that under the Income Tax Act is taxed on Canadian-source income through a permanent establishment. Hybrid mismatch rules under the Income Tax Act generally deny deductions for payments characterized differently in other jurisdictions, and an election can be made under section 216 (for certain rental or timber income), subsection 115.1 (for dispositions by non-residents), or by treaty tie-breaker resolution through the mutual agreement procedure; there is no general 'check-the-box' election.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Goods and Services Tax / Harmonized Sales Tax (GST/HST) and British Columbia Provincial Sales Tax (PST)
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000 in worldwide taxable supplies over any four consecutive calendar quarters (GST/HST registration threshold under Excise Tax Act); for British Columbia PST, there is no registration threshold — every seller making taxable sales of goods or taxable services in BC must register. Additionally, a non-resident vendor that is a 'non-registered non-resident' may be required to register if it solicits orders in BC or delivers goods into BC. For the GST/HST, small supplier status exceptions may apply; once registered, GST at 5% federal rate applies in BC (no provincial HST component because BC uses a separate PST).
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: Canada currently does not mandate a real-time fiscal clearance, continuous transaction control (CTC), or digital stamping regime for standard e-invoicing in the private sector. The CRA has implemented mandatory electronic reporting requirements for digital platform operators under Part IX of the Excise Tax Act, but there is no universal mandatory e-invoicing API clearance mandate. Tax invoices (GST/HST) must contain prescribed information under the Excise Tax Act (e.g., vendor name, BN/GST/HST registration number, date of invoice, consideration, tax rate, and tax amount). Since July 2020, federal GST/HST returns and certain filings must be filed electronically, but that is not an e-invoice clearance obligation. Businesses may use EDI or XML invoices, and the CRA accepts electronic records; however, no pre-clearance digital stamp is required. For BC PST, vendors are required to issue a sales invoice containing prescribed PST information, maintain records, and report through the BC eTaxBC portal; there is no fiscal stamping.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Exports of qualifying medical-grade nitrile examination gloves are generally zero-rated under section 1 of Part V of Schedule VI to the Excise Tax Act, provided the goods are exported by the supplier for supply outside Canada, or delivered outside Canada by common carrier or freight forwarder, and are not acquired for use in Canada. Suppliers must maintain evidence of export within a reasonable time; supplies of goods made by a registrant who exports them are zero-rated when the supplier satisfies the CRA that the goods were exported as part of the supply. Additionally, services performed on exported goods and certain transportation services may qualify for zero-rating. The supplier may claim input tax credits (ITCs) on the inputs attributable to zero-rated exports, resulting in a net refund of the GST/HST paid on purchases. No provincial PST zero-rating exists for exports from BC; the PST is generally not applied to goods delivered outside Canada by the vendor, but the vendor should retain documentation of delivery to a point outside Canada. Under Part IX of the Excise Tax Act, the exporter must not be a non-registrant making a false representation to obtain a rebate, and the exported goods must not be acquired for consumption or supply in Canada.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Canada Customs Export Declaration (Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) Form B13A, or automated export declaration through the Canadian Export Reporting System (CAED)/CEX)
Proof of the commercial invoice and sale contract evidencing sale to a non-resident
Bill of Lading (B/L) or air waybill showing the foreign destination and delivery outside Canada
Canadian Bankers Association (CBA) / bank inward remittance certificate or SWIFT/TT wire confirmation evidencing payment in foreign currency
Packing slip and HS classification certificate confirming the goods are 39.13 / 40.15 category eligible nitrile gloves (HS 4015.12) and sterile medical classification, if applicable
Customs power of attorney / broker authorization where export clearance is completed by a licensed customs broker
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: The CRA may reassess a zero-rated supply to taxable (reversing the zero-rating and requiring GST/HST at 5% or the provincial component) if the exporter fails to substantiate the export with adequate documentation or exports are not supported by the goods leaving Canada in keeping with section 143 and Schedule VI, Part V of the Excise Tax Act. Penalties under the Excise Tax Act may include a 'gross negligence penalty' of 50% of the tax payable (recoverable amount) or, where the exporter knowingly or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence files a false statement, penalties under subsection 285(2) (i.e., the greater of CAD 250 and 25% of the additional tax payable), plus interest and arrears on any net tax due. Fraudulent claims can result in criminal prosecution under the Income Tax Act (tax evasion penalty of 50% of the tax evaded and imprisonment up to two years) and the Crown Liability and Proceedings Act. Additionally, under subsection 297(1), a person who issues a false invoice or supplies false information in relation to a rebate may be liable to a penalty of CAD 2,000 or, if the false claim is made knowingly, a fine up to 250% of the amount of the rebate claimed. CRA export verification programs routinely scrutinize high-risk refund claims, and the exporter must retain books and records for six years; the limitation period for reassessment for non-residents is generally three years from the date of the notice of assessment, extended to four years where estate or trust issues arise, and indefinitely in the case of misrepresentation or fraud. Clawbacks may include the loss of the export zero-rating retroactively plus interest, and penalties of up to 25% of the amount of tax for due diligence failures; repeated serious failures may trigger a customs compliance verification by the CBSA, and liability for the export transaction may be assumed by the exporter, customs broker, or consignor.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada); there is no dedicated foreign-exchange control administration in Canada. Exchange-rate and FX policy are administered by the Department of Finance Canada in coordination with the Bank of Canada, while prudential supervision of authorized banks is exercised by the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI).
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: Canada maintains full currency convertibility for both current-account and capital-account transactions under IMF Article VIII. There are no exchange controls, no central-bank prior-approval requirements, and no statutory profit-remittance hurdles for a qualifying business corporation. Outbound dividend distributions are subject to Part XIII withholding tax at the domestic rate of 25%, reducible under applicable income-tax treaties (e.g., 5%-15% under the Canada-US Convention and equivalent agreements); interest and royalty cross-border payments are similarly treaty-eligible. All cross-border fund movements are monitored only through (i) reporting obligations under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (PCMLTFA), including large-transaction reports to FINTRAC, and (ii) balance-of-payments statistical reporting by the receiving/remitting bank to the Bank of Canada and Statistics Canada. No exchange-control approval certificates are required for capital injection, trade settlement, or distribution.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: None. Canada imposes no statutory timeline, no mandatory conversion ratio, and no surrender obligation on export receipts. A British Columbia medical-PPE exporter may retain export proceeds in the invoiced currency, hold CAD, USD, or foreign-currency operating accounts domestically or with an offshore affiliate, and freely determine the timing and means of conversion to CAD. The only applicable duties are general corporate record-keeping requirements for tax, customs (CBSA), and equipment-leasing documentation under the Income Tax Act and the Customs Act.

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Capital Escrow Account / Operational Concentration Account with USD sub-ledger for export proceeds
Capital Escrow Account / Business Operating Account with Foreign Currency (USD) sweep
Capital Escrow Account / Operational Account integrated with trade-finance desk (LC/BD)
Capital Escrow Account / Operational Account with Cross-Border Banking unit for daily FX conversion
Operational Account / Global Banking USD-CAD multi-currency treasury package

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.bank_name: HSBC Bank Canada (legacy entity merged into RBC as of Q1 2024; migration portfolio)
tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Legacy Capital Escrow Account / Legacy Operational Account being converted to RBC platforms

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Low feasibility as a primary corporate treasury bank. Canada does not licence fintech electronic-money institutions (EMIs) as bank-class institutions: deposit-taking and full corporate banking powers are reserved exclusively for Schedule I and Schedule II banks under the Bank Act (Canada), which are federally chartered and CDIC-insured. Offshore digital EMIs (e.g., Wise, Revolut, or comparable platforms) may lawfully operate only as money-services businesses (MSBs) registered with FINTRAC under the PCMLTFA; they are permitted to offer cross-border remittance and FX conversion but cannot provide escrow accounts, regulated overdraft facilities, commercial letters of credit, or chequing services. Such platforms may be used as a secondary, low-value remittance rail for supplier test payments, but the holding and disbursement of material export proceeds and capital injections must be managed through a tier-1 domestic bank, with the EMI route subject to a documented risk assessment in the treasury policy.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Statutorily, physical presence is not mandated under the PCMLTFA: identity verification may be completed via the two-factor or combined methods (e.g., credit-file check matched against passport data, or dual authorized-signatory confirmation). In practice, the Big Six Canadian banks require at least one director with signing authority — and ordinarily the ultimate beneficial owner (UBO) — to complete either an in-person interview or a video-interview session at a branch commercial bank centre; several banks will decline fully remote onboarding for foreign-controlled newly incorporated companies. The recommended protocol for this BC entity is to arrange an in-person KYC interview at a Vancouver commercial banking centre with the owning director present, followed by notarized authorization permitting remote delegated onboarding of co-signers and the bank's foreign-exchange and trade-services officers.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Complex layered ownership structure with a foreign parent or multiple intermediate holding vehicles triggering UBO red flags
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Certified certificate of incorporation (federal or BC), complete corporate organizational chart identifying every natural-person UBO with percentage ownership and control rights, certified register of directors, certified register of shareholders, registered-office address, and a legal-entity identifier (LEI) if held; where the parent is audited, include the latest consolidated financial statements.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Non-resident directors, foreign-source initial capital, and large inbound wire transfers at account opening
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Valid passports and proof of residential address for each director and UBO, tax identification numbers (TIN) for each relevant jurisdiction, foreign bank reference letter, 12-month source-of-funds bank statements, executed share subscription agreement, and a board resolution authorising the capital injection and describing the projected use of funds.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Ultimate beneficial owners resident or incorporated in a FATF-monitored or higher-risk jurisdiction
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Independent legal opinion from a licensed Canadian solicitor confirming ownership legitimacy, a completed bank enhanced-due-diligence questionnaire (EDDQ), sanctioned-party screening evidence for all directors and counterparties, and documentary proof of real commercial activity — including the production facility lease and purchase orders from medical distributors.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Newly formed manufacturing company projecting high transaction volumes and USD export receipts without prior revenue history
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Bankable business plan and 24-month cash-flow forecast, evidence of facility control (lease or land title certificate), Health Canada Medical Device Establishment Licence (MDEL), ISO 13485 certificate, and firm commercial contracts or letters of intent from glove distributors together with supplier quotations for raw materials and machinery.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Inability of the investor to demonstrate source of wealth for the subscribed share capital
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Audited financial statements or a verified net-worth statement of the subscribing shareholder, foreign tax-return proof, signed client KYC questionnaire, statutory declaration as to source of wealth, and completion of the bank's source-of-wealth questionnaire with supporting records of the disposal or dividend that funded the contribution.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Compliant wire transfer protocol: the foreign parent or investor effects the equity injection via SWIFT MT103 (single payment) or MT202 (interbank cover) with the beneficiary as the BC corporation and a narrative stating 'Share capital contribution — subscription price for [number] of common shares of [issuer legal name]'. Canada requires no prior FX approval; the receiving bank classifies the payment as inward direct investment under the balance-of-payments statistical framework (equity capital component) and credits the operating account or a dedicated capital escrow account. The corporation must hold: (i) a directors' resolution authorizing the issuance and allotment; (ii) a countersigned share subscription agreement; (iii) an updated register of shareholders filed with the BC Registrar of Companies on the next annual report; and (iv) accounting recognition of the equity instrument under IFRS 2 / IAS 32. For exports, no special purpose code is mandated in the same manner as under an exchange-control regime; the bank requires only a supporting narrative reflecting the invoice or contract reference, though FINTRAC large-transaction reporting thresholds apply (record for transactions at or above CAD 10,000; report suspicious transactions and cross-border transfers of currency or monetary instruments at or above CAD 10,000). Verification at account opening includes provision of the executed subscription agreement and a notarized identification statement from the funding bank confirming the origin of the wire.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Clearing rails for trade settlements: (1) SWIFT MT103 direct telegraphic transfers for supplier payments where counterparties accept T/T terms — appropriate for chemical feedstock, coagulation additives, packaging materials, and miscellaneous customs charges; (2) commercial irrevocable letters of credit issued via SWIFT MT700/MT707 for high-value machinery and major raw-material contracts, with settlement by presentation of compliant documents and interbank reimbursement via SWIFT MT103/MT202; (3) documentary collections (documents-against-payment D/P or documents-against-acceptance D/A) using SWIFT MT4xx/MT5xx as a cost-reduced alternative for repeat suppliers; (4) USD domestic clearing through correspondent bank networks (CHIPS and Fedwire) for USD-denominated payments within the United States; and (5) CAD domestic clearing through Payments Canada (LVTS and ACSS) for inland disbursements such as payroll, utilities, and Canadian suppliers. The treasury policy should route all major outflows through the BC operating concentration account, with the bank's trade-services desk confirming each LC, and all export receipts from medical-PPE customers repatriated by SWIFT MT103 into the same concentration account to preserve liquidity visibility and reduce FX conversion leakage.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable USD/CAD forward contracts (plain vanilla, standard tenors of 1, 3, 6, 9, and 12 months) documented under an ISDA Master Agreement or bilateral FX confirmation
FX swaps (spot-forward rollovers) to manage inter-month working-capital mismatches between USD export receipts and CAD operating disbursements
Cross-currency swaps (CCIRS / long-date currency swaps) hedging long-term USD-denominated machinery capex and export financing
Vanilla and zero-cost collar FX options on USD/CAD to cap conversion cost while retaining upside on favourable rates
Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) on permitted cross-pairs where physical CAD delivery is operationally impractical, noting that CAD is freely convertible and deliverable in all standard market tenors

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: BC Annual Report (Corporate Registry annual existence and records return)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: BC Corporate Registry, Registry Services, Ministry of Finance (Victoria, British Columbia)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 2 calendar months after the anniversary date of the corporation's incorporation; late filing is available after the anniversary but before the next anniversary.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing fee of CAD 150 (approximate USD 110); failure to file for two consecutive reporting anniversaries permits the Registrar to administratively dissolve or cancel the company; restoration fee of CAD 300 (approximate USD 220) plus all outstanding arrears and required filings.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: T2 Corporation Income Tax Return with financial statements and applicable schedules
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 6 months after the corporation's fiscal year-end; balance-due day is 3 months after fiscal year-end for an eligible Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) claiming the small business deduction, otherwise 2 months after fiscal year-end.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late-filing penalty of 5% of the unpaid balance plus 1% per complete month of delay up to 12 months (minimum CAD 250 for nil-balance returns); daily compound prescribed-rate interest; gross-negligence penalty under Income Tax Act s. 163(2); continued non-filing may lead to enforcement, garnishment, and director liability for unremitted amounts.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: T4 Information Slips and T4 Summary of Remuneration Paid (payroll year-end return)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: On or before February 28 of the calendar year following the payroll year (February 29 in a leap year).
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Penalty of CAD 25 per slip per day of lateness (minimum CAD 100, maximum CAD 2,500); T4 Summary late filing CAD 25 per day up to CAD 2,500; knowingly false slips attract a CAD 100 per slip penalty; interest and director liability may apply to unremitted payroll source deductions.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: GST/HST Annual Return (Form GST34) for annual filers, with quarterly instalments where applicable
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 3 months after the fiscal year-end for annual filers; quarterly instalments due within 1 month after each fiscal quarter where net GST/HST payable exceeds CAD 3,000.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late-filing penalty under Excise Tax Act s. 280(1): 5% of the unpaid net GST/HST plus 1% per complete month up to 12 months; daily compound prescribed-rate interest; failure to file after demand may result in CRA field collection, asset seizure, and director liability.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: BC Employer Health Tax (EHT) Annual Return
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: BC Ministry of Finance (Taxpayer Services, Victoria, British Columbia)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: On or before March 31 following the calendar year-end; applies only where annual BC payroll exceeds CAD 500,000, with a 2.925% rate on total BC remuneration above the exemption threshold; no return required below the threshold.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late-filing penalty of 10% of the tax shown on the return; daily compound arrears interest at the prescribed quarterly rate; recovery includes set-off against provincial payments and potential director liability for unremitted employer health tax.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: No mandatory annual statutory financial audit is imposed by the BC Business Corporations Act (SBC 2002, c. 62) on a non-distributing private company absent contractual or regulatory obligation; a statutory audit is triggered where shareholders holding at least 25% of the issued voting shares requisition an audit (BC BCA s. 203), where the corporation is a distributing/public company, where institutional creditors or regulators contractually require certified statements, or where ISO 13485 quality-system certification and Health Canada Medical Device Establishment Licence inspection evidence require independently reviewed or audited financials; for a mid-sized nitrile glove manufacturer, audit obligation is therefore driven by shareholder requisition, lender covenants, or procurement/regulatory conditions rather than a revenue or asset filing threshold.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: IFRS (Part I of the CPA Canada Handbook) is mandatory for publicly accountable enterprises; private BC corporations may adopt ASPE (Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises, Part II of the CPA Canada Handbook); compiled or notice-to-reader unaudited financial statements are generally accepted for CRA and BC Registry filings, although the T2 Corporation Income Tax Return must attach applicable financial statements in the prescribed format.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: For a BC provincial corporation, the individuals with significant control transparency register (BC BCA Part 6.2) must be accurate and updated within 15 days of any share transfer creating a new significant-control person or any change to registered particulars; the BC annual report filed with the Registrar confirms corporate existence and records-office details but does not constitute a public annual UBO declaration comparable to federal CBCA filings; law enforcement, the CRA, and the BC Registrar may demand production of the transparency register on request, and the company must permit prescribed inspection at its records office; failure to maintain or produce the register attracts offence-level penalties and daily fines.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of Members, Register of Directors, Minute Book

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: USD 80–250 per annum (typical Vancouver/BC market range for registered records office, corporate agent services, and annual-report preparation, exclusive of government fees and disbursements)
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: USD 10,000–35,000 per annum for a mid-sized manufacturing private corporation where a certified audit is contractually required or shareholder-requisitioned; compiled notice-to-reader financial statements by a CPA firm generally range USD 3,000–7,000 per annum.

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 27% combined general (15% federal + 12% British Columbia); 11% combined for eligible CCPC active business income up to the C$500,000 small business deduction limit (9% federal + 2% BC).
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: Federal SR&ED investment tax credit of 35% refundable (CCPC limits) or 15% non-refundable for other corporations on qualified scientific research and experimental development expenditures; BC SR&ED tax credit of 10% of eligible expenditures (refundable for CCPCs, capped at C$300,000 per year); 100% Capital Cost Allowance for eligible manufacturing and processing property under the Accelerated Investment Incentive; no separate patent-box; the general 15% federal rate reduction already applies to all federal taxable income.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: T2 Corporation Income Tax Return; e-filed through CRA-approved tax preparation software (T2 e-File) or via CRA My Business Account; provincial corporate tax for British Columbia is reported on the same federal T2 under the Canada–BC Tax Collection Agreement.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual; a T2 must be filed for each taxation year regardless of taxable income or whether any tax is payable.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Due date is six months after the taxation year-end. Balance-due day (payment deadline) is two months after the year-end for most non-CCPCs, and three months after year-end for CCPCs eligible for the small business deduction (subject to associated-corporate taxable income thresholds).

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: The 15-character BN (e.g., 123456789 RC0001) identifying the corporation, including the RC program account for corporate income tax.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident corporations carrying on business in Canada through a permanent establishment must use the BN assigned to the Canadian branch and identify the agent for service in Canada.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: The fiscal period covered by the return; the period cannot exceed 12 months unless an approved year-end change applies.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident corporations should align the Canadian taxation year with the foreign fiscal year under section 249 where permitted, and attach a reconciliation of foreign and Canadian taxation years.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Accounting net income before income tax computed under IFRS or ASPE in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, as presented in the financial statements.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Reconcile foreign GAAP differences to Canadian GAAP; the Canadian-booked branch income used for tax must reflect the separately booked Canadian business income.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Lines 200/300 – Net Income (Loss) for Income Tax Purposes
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Accounting income adjusted for permanent and timing differences, including capital cost allowance (CCA), reserves, SR&ED expenditures, and other non-deductible items.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Add back Part XIII taxes and head-office expense allocations not properly attributed to the Canadian permanent establishment; deduct treaty-exempt items only where a valid treaty claim exists.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: The amount subject to federal Part I income tax after application of non-capital loss carryforwards and the federal small business deduction allocation.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Use the Canadian-source taxable income attributable to the Canadian branch; do not claim foreign losses or foreign exempt surplus items on this line.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Federal tax computed at the applicable statutory rate (15% general or 9% on the small business deduction base), before investment tax credits and refundable credits.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For a non-resident corporation, only Canadian-source business income is taxed; treaty-relief items are excluded from the calculation.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Provincial corporate tax calculated on taxable income allocated to British Columbia under the BC allocation and attribution rules; BC rates are 12% general or 2% small business.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: If the non-resident has permanent establishments both inside and outside BC, allocate gross revenue and salaries under the BC Income Tax Act allocation regulations and attach the apportionment schedule.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: The net amount payable after instalments, estimated payments, refundable investment tax credits, and other credits, or the refund owing to the corporation.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Refundable credits (e.g., refundable SR&ED ITCs) are available only for Canadian-source eligible activity; cross-border refund claims are subject to CRA non-resident certification and enforcement safeguards.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Schedule 25 / Form T106 – Transfer Pricing Cross-Reference
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Schedule 25 summarizes the arm's-length transfer pricing methods applied; Form T106 reports non-arm's-length transactions with non-residents.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident controlled Canadian subsidiaries must contemporaneously document that the purchase price of nitrile glove raw materials, the sale price of finished gloves, and intercompany management fees are arm's length.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing of the T2 triggers a penalty of 5% of the balance owing plus 1% per full month late (maximum 12 months); a repeat late-filing assessment rises to 10% plus 2% per month (maximum 20 months). Unpaid tax and penalties accrue compounded daily interest at CRA prescribed rates (currently 9% per annum). Separate penalties apply for late T106 transfer pricing disclosure (C$25/day to C$2,500; C$100/day to C$12,500 for false statements), and willful non-filing can result in criminal prosecution with fines and imprisonment.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 25% Part XIII tax on dividends paid or credited by a Canadian resident corporation to a non-resident shareholder; applies to gross dividends regardless of the payer's profit level.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To apply a treaty rate: (1) obtain a Certificate of Residence (TRC) from the foreign tax authority; (2) complete CRA Form NR301 (U.S. residents), NR302 (residents of treaty countries other than the U.S.), or NR303 as applicable; (3) submit the certified residence certificate and fully executed form to the Canadian corporate payer before dividend remittance; (4) the payer then withholds at the reduced treaty rate (typically 5% for a U.S. corporate shareholder holding at least 10% of voting shares; 15% for portfolio shareholders), subject to the Canada–U.S. treaty beneficial-ownership and purpose tests; (5) retain the TRC and forms in corporate records for six years. If over-withholding occurred, the non-resident must file a refund claim with the CRA within the applicable two-year statutory window.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Domestic Part XIII rate: 25% on royalties and 25% on interest paid to non-residents (subject to exceptions for arm's-length interest, exempt interest on long-term corporate bonds, and certain other specific categories). Under the Canada–U.S. Tax Treaty, royalties for patents, trademarks, and industrial know-how are taxed at 10% (0% for literary, dramatic, musical or artistic copyright royalties, including software in certain cases), and interest paid at arm's length to U.S. residents is generally exempt from Canadian withholding; portfolio interest and participating interest may be treated differently. The statutory rate prevails absent proper treaty documentation.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: Form T106 (Information Return of Non-Arm's Length Transactions with Non-Residents) must be filed when the aggregate value of transactions with any one non-resident non-arm's-length person exceeds C$1,000,000 in a taxation year. CRA Information Circular 87-2R requires contemporaneous transfer pricing documentation. The Local File is the Canadian transfer pricing documentation package; the OECD Chapter V Master File equivalent is not statutorily required for all taxpayers, but Country-by-Country reporting (Form RC4649) is mandatory for ultimate parent entities of MNE groups with consolidated group revenue of C$750,000,000 or more.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Canada does not apply Gulf-state style Economic Substance Regulations; however, economic substance is tested through the statutory General Anti-Avoidance Rule (section 245), the 'business purpose' and 'sham' doctrines at common law, and the transfer pricing 'reality' principle in section 247(2). For cross-border structures, the Canada–U.S. treaty's beneficial ownership and purpose tests, plus Canada's foreign affiliate dumping rules (section 212.3), require a resident corporation to demonstrate real employees, real operational activities, and actual risk assumption. A BC-resident entity with no office, no staff, and no purchasing or production functions in respect of nitrile glove dipping contracts will be disregarded or recharacterized, with the tax benefit reversed.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Tax Evasion / False Statements (Income Tax Act s.239)
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Wilfully making false or misleading statements in the T2, failing to report Canadian-source income, destroying books and records, or knowingly omitting revenue from disposals of nitrile glove production lines or export sales to related overseas distributors.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: On indictment, imprisonment for up to five years plus a fine of not less than 50% and not more than 200% of the tax sought to be evaded; on summary conviction, a fine and/or imprisonment of up to two years. The tax, interest, and gross-negligence penalties (50%) remain collectible, and CRA has statutory power to seize bank accounts and freeze assets.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who authorize or participate in the misstatement are personally liable under section 227.1 for unremitted source deductions and GST/HST, and as parties to the offense they may face criminal conviction, court-ordered restitution, travel restrictions, and removal from corporate office.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Transfer Pricing Misstatement / Deficiency (Income Tax Act s.247(3))
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failure to prepare and retain contemporaneous transfer pricing documentation; non-arm's-length pricing of glove purchase allocations, intercompany management fees, or royalties paid to an offshore IP company; absence of a valid TP policy for raw-material purchases from a non-resident affiliate.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: A 10% penalty on the net transfer pricing adjustment, plus full reassessment of income, compounded daily interest, and loss of loss-carryforward erosion if the adjustment re-characterizes transactions.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who sign the T106 with false statements are exposed to the criminal sanctions of section 239; civil restitution may be sought for dividends distributed while the corporation was insolvent after a TP adjustment.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Shell Company / GAAR and Treaty Abuse
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Using a BC-resident corporation with no economic substance as a conduit to obtain an artificially low dividend withholding rate, round-tripping dividends through a U.S. holding company with no commercial activity, or executing a circular financing arrangement that strips taxable surplus out of Canada without arm's-length consideration.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The tax benefit is denied entirely; the CRA reassesses and recaptures the avoided tax plus compound interest; a gross-negligence penalty of 50% of the understated federal tax may be imposed under section 163(2), and in cross-border cases the CRA may apply a general anti-avoidance penalty equal to 25% of the denied benefit where the avoidance is supported by misrepresentation.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors responsible for the artificial structure may be assessed as co-conspirators in a fraudulent conveyance if assets were transferred abroad to defeat CRA collection; personal liability and travel bans can be ordered by the court under collection proceedings.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: AML / FINTRAC Compliance (PCMLTFA; Criminal Code s.462.31)
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: A glove trading entity accepting cash settlement in excess of C$10,000 without filing a Large Cash Transaction Report, failing to register with FINTRAC if engaged in money services (e.g., collecting Swift/LC fees in foreign jurisdictions), or failing to report a suspicious payment transiting through high-risk conduits.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Administrative monetary penalties up to C$500,000 for a first contravention and up to C$1,000,000 for subsequent contraventions; criminal prosecution for money laundering under the Criminal Code carries imprisonment up to 10 years and fines in the court's discretion; assets are subject to restraint and forfeiture orders.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Officers and directors who knowingly direct or tolerate the laundering scheme face personal criminal liability, imprisonment up to 10 years, individual fines, and travel bans; professional licenses of directors and beneficial owners can be revoked.
